location.value: Western Europe, gradually expanding from the Paris region to roughly modern France. Colonies included New France, the Caribbean and Indian trading posts.

terrain.value: Fertile plains and river basins (Seine, Loire, Rhône), with the Pyrenees, Alps and Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts as natural borders.
terrain.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

climate.value: Temperate. Harsh winters and harvest failures (e.g. 1693–94, 1709, 1788) caused famines.
climate.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

resources.value: Europe’s largest farming population, wine, grain, and textiles.
resources.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

disasters.value: The Black Death (1348). Famines in 1693–94 and the Great Frost of 1709.
disasters.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

population.value: Not in the Wikipedia infobox. France was Europe’s most populous kingdom, with about 20 million people around 1700 and 28 million by 1789.
population.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

urbanisation.value: Paris was its capital and largest city, one of Europe’s largest. The court was at Versailles from 1682 to 1789.

disease.value: The Black Death (1348) killed perhaps a third of the people; plague returned often until 1720 (Marseille).
disease.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

migration.value: Persecuted Protestants (Huguenots) fled after the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685.
migration.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

economicBase.value: Agriculture, plus manufactures promoted by the state (Colbert’s mercantilism) and colonial trade.
economicBase.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

tradeRoutes.value: Colonial trade with the Caribbean (sugar plantations using enslaved Africans), India, the Levant and New France’s fur trade.

wealth.value: No GDP figure is given in the sources checked. One of Europe’s largest economies, but with heavy state debt.

moneyAndTax.value: The livre tournois, louis d’or and écu. Taxes fell mostly on commoners, and debt from wars (especially the American War of Independence) created the financial crisis of the 1780s.

inequality.value: Clergy and nobles were largely tax-exempt, while the Third Estate (commoners) carried most of the burden, a cause of the Revolution.
inequality.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy (987–1791), then briefly a constitutional monarchy (1791–92), and again after 1814.

keyRulers.value: Hugh Capet (987–996). Philip II Augustus. Louis IX. Francis I. Henry IV. Louis XIV, the “Sun King” (1643–1715). Louis XVI (1774–1792).

succession.value: Hereditary, by male primogeniture (Salic law), through the Capetian, Valois and Bourbon dynasties.

institutions.value: The Estates General (from 1302, not called between 1614 and 1789), the parlements (law courts), and royal intendants. The Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (1539) made French the language of law.

stability.value: The Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453), the Wars of Religion (1562–1598), the Fronde (1648–53), and the French Revolution (1789).

eliteConflict.value: Royal centralisation against powerful nobles (the Fronde) and the parlements, and later aristocratic resistance to tax reform.

armyAndTech.value: Under Louis XIV, the largest standing army in Europe and Vauban’s fortifications.
armyAndTech.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

majorWars.value: The Hundred Years’ War. The Italian Wars. The Thirty Years’ War. The wars of Louis XIV (including the War of the Spanish Succession, 1701–14). The Seven Years’ War. Support for American independence.

territoryChange.value: Gained Normandy (1204), Burgundy (1477), Alsace, Franche-Comté, Lorraine (1766) and Corsica (1769). Lost New France to Britain after the Seven Years’ War (1763).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: England/Britain, the Habsburgs and Spain. Allies: the Ottomans (16th century), Scotland (the “Auld Alliance”) and the American revolutionaries.

inventions.value: Science under royal patronage: the Académie des sciences (1666) and the Paris Observatory. Pascal, Descartes, Lavoisier.
inventions.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

scienceEducation.value: The University of Paris (Sorbonne) and the Enlightenment’s Encyclopédie (Diderot, d’Alembert).
scienceEducation.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

openness.value: A cultural leader of Europe, but with censorship and religious persecution (e.g. revoking the Edict of Nantes in 1685).
openness.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

religion.value: Roman Catholicism (majority and official), with a Protestant (Huguenot) minority tolerated under the Edict of Nantes (1598–1685).

languageWriting.value: Latin, then French (official in law from 1539), plus regional languages such as Breton, Occitan and Basque.

artsArchitecture.value: Gothic cathedrals (Chartres, Notre-Dame), the Palace of Versailles, and classical literature (Molière, Racine) and Enlightenment writers (Voltaire, Rousseau).
artsArchitecture.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

socialStructure.value: Three estates: clergy, nobility and the Third Estate (bourgeoisie, artisans and peasants).

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Catholic king. A national identity grew through the Hundred Years’ War (Joan of Arc) and the French language.
sharedIdentity.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

neighbours.value: England, the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, the Italian states, the Dutch Republic and Savoy.

ideasReligions.value: Exported court culture, the French language (the language of European diplomacy) and Enlightenment ideas.
ideasReligions.source: Jones, The Cambridge Illustrated History of France (1994)

colonisation.value: The first French colonial empire: New France (Quebec, from 1608), Caribbean slave colonies (Saint-Domingue), and posts in India and Senegal. By the 1680s it covered about 10 million km².

riseSignals.value: The Capetian dynasty slowly extended royal control over the great fiefs. Victory in the Hundred Years’ War (1453). Strong central administration.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Louis XIV (1643–1715), Europe’s dominant power.

declineSignals.value: Debt from costly wars, an unfair tax system, poor harvests (1788) and aristocratic resistance to reform.

outcome.value: Revolution. The French Revolution (1789) abolished the monarchy on 21 September 1792 and created the First Republic. The monarchy was briefly restored from 1814 to 1848.

sources.value: Royal archives, chronicles, and the writings of the Ancien Régime and the Revolution. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (mostly the infobox). See also Jones (1994).

overallCertainty.value: Good. The start is dated 843 (Treaty of Verdun) or 987 (Hugh Capet). Population and economic figures are estimates.
